rules.text: design frameworks that are both powerful and easy to use.
understand and explicitly design for a broad range of developers with different programming styles, requirements, and skill levels.
understand and design for the broad variety of programming languages.
make sure that the API design specification is the central part of the design of any feature that includes a publicly accessible API.
define top usage scenarios for each major feature area.
ensure that the scenarios correspond to an appropriate abstraction level. They should roughly correspond to the end-user use cases.
design APIs by first writing code samples for the main scenarios and then defining the object model to support the code samples.
write main scenario code samples in at least two different language families (e.g., C# and F#).
writing main scenario code samples using a dynamically typed language such as PowerShell or IronPython.
rely solely on standard design methodologies when designing the public API layer of a framework.
organize usability studies to test APIs in main scenarios.
ensure that each main feature area namespace contains only types that are used in the most common scenarios. Types used in advanced scenarios should be placed in subnamespaces.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: provide simple overloads of constructors and methods. A simple overload has a very small number of parameters, and all parameters are primitives.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: have members intended for advanced scenarios on types intended for mainline scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: require users to explicitly instantiate more than one type in the most basic scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: require that users perform any extensive initialization before they can start programming basic scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: provide good defaults for all properties and parameters (using convenience overloads), if possible.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: communicate incorrect usage of APIs using exceptions.
rules.section: 2.2.2 The Principle of Low Barrier to Entry

rules.text: ensure that APIs are intuitive and can be successfully used in basic scenarios without referring to the reference documentation.
rules.section: 2.2.3 The Principle of Self-Documenting Object Models

rules.text: provide great documentation with all APIs.
rules.section: 2.2.3 The Principle of Self-Documenting Object Models

rules.text: provide code samples illustrating how to use your most important APIs in common scenarios.
rules.section: 2.2.3 The Principle of Self-Documenting Object Models

rules.text: make the discussion about identifier naming choices a significant part of specification reviews.
be afraid to use verbose identifier names when doing so makes the API self-documenting.
involving technical writers early in the design process. They can be a great resource for spotting designs with bad name choices and designs that would be difficult to explain to users.
reserving the best type names for the most commonly used types.
use exception messages to communicate framework usage mistakes to the developer.
provide strongly typed APIs if at all possible.
ensure consistency with .NET and other frameworks your users are likely to interact with.
many abstractions in mainline-scenario APIs.
using a layered framework with high-level APIs optimized for productivity, and using low-level APIs optimized for power and expressiveness.
rules.section: 2.2.4.2 Exposing Layers in the Same Namespace

rules.text: mixing low-level and high-level APIs in a single namespace if the low-level APIs are very complex (i.e., they contain many types).
rules.section: 2.2.4.2 Exposing Layers in the Same Namespace

rules.text: ensure that layers of a single feature area are well integrated. Developers should be able to start programming using one of the layers and then change their code to use the other layer without rewriting the whole application.
rules.section: 2.2.4.2 Exposing Layers in the Same Namespace

rules.text: use PascalCasing for the names of namespaces, types, members, and generic type parameters.
use camelCasing for parameter names.
capitalize both characters of two-character acronyms, except the first word of a camel-cased identifier.
capitalize only the first character of acronyms with three or more characters, except the first word of a camel-cased identifier.
capitalize any of the characters of any acronyms, whatever their length, at the beginning of a camel-cased identifier.
capitalize each word in so-called closed-form compound words.
rules.section: 3.1.3 Capitalizing Compound Words and Common Terms

rules.text: assume that all programming languages are case sensitive. They are not. Names cannot differ by case alone.
choose easily readable identifier names.
favor readability over brevity. The property name `CanScrollHorizontally` is better than `ScrollableX` (an obscure reference to the *X*-axis).
use underscores, hyphens, or any other non-alphanumeric characters.
use Hungarian notation.
using identifiers that conflict with keywords of widely used programming languages.
use only ASCII characters in identifier names.
use abbreviations or contractions as part of identifier names.
use any acronyms that are not widely accepted, and even if they are, only when necessary.
use semantically interesting names rather than language-specific keywords for type names.
use a generic CLR type name, rather than a language-specific name, in the rare cases when an identifier has no semantic meaning beyond its type.
use a common name, such as *value* or *item*, rather than repeating the type name, in the rare cases when an identifier has no semantic meaning and the type of the parameter is not important.
use a name similar to the old API when creating new versions of an existing API.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: prefer adding a suffix rather than a prefix to indicate a new version of an existing API.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: using a brand-new, but meaningful, identifier, instead of adding a suffix or a prefix.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: use a numeric suffix to indicate a new version of an existing API, particularly if the existing name of the API is the only name that makes sense (e.g., if it is an industry standard) and if adding any meaningful suffix (or changing the name) is not an appropriate option.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: use the “Ex” (or a similar) suffix for an identifier to distinguish it from an earlier version of the same API.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: use the “64” suffix when introducing versions of APIs that operate on a 64-bit integer (a long integer) instead of a 32-bit integer. You only need to take this approach when the existing 32-bit API exists; don’t do it for brand-new APIs with only a 64-bit version.
rules.section: 3.2.4 Naming New Versions of Existing APIs

rules.text: choose names for your assembly DLLs that suggest large chunks of functionality, such as `System.Data`.
rules.section: 3.3 Names of Assemblies, DLLs, and Packages

rules.text: prefix namespace names with a company name to prevent namespaces from different companies from having the same name.
use a stable, version-independent product name at the second level of a namespace name.

use organizational hierarchies as the basis for names in namespace hierarchies, because group names within corporations tend to be short-lived. Organize the hierarchy of namespaces around groups of related technologies.

use PascalCasing, and separate namespace components with periods (e.g., `Microsoft.Office.PowerPoint`). If your brand employs nontraditional casing, you should follow the casing defined by your brand, even if it deviates from normal namespace casing.
using plural namespace names where appropriate.
use the same name for a namespace and a type in that namespace.
introduce overly general type names such as `Element`, `Node`, `Log`, and `Message`.
give the same name to multiple types across namespaces within a single application model.
give types names that would conflict with any type in the core namespaces.
assign type names that would conflict with other types within a single technology.
introduce type name conflicts between types in technology namespaces and an application model namespace (unless the technology is not expected to be used with the application model).
name classes and structs with nouns or noun phrases, using PascalCasing.
rules.section: 3.5 Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

rules.text: name interfaces with adjective phrases, or occasionally with nouns or noun phrases.
rules.section: 3.5 Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

rules.text: give class names a prefix (e.g., “C”).
rules.section: 3.5 Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

rules.text: ending the name of derived classes with the name of the base class.
rules.section: 3.5 Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

rules.text: prefix interface names with the letter *I*, to indicate that the type is an interface.
rules.section: 3.5 Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

rules.text: ensure that the names differ only by the “I” prefix on the interface name when you are defining a class–interface pair where the class is a standard implementation of the interface.
rules.section: 3.5 Names of Classes, Structs, and Interfaces

rules.text: name generic type parameters with descriptive names unless a single-letter name is completely self-explanatory and a descriptive name would not add value.
using `T` as the type parameter name for types with one single-letter type parameter.
prefix descriptive type parameter names with `T`.
indicating constraints placed on a type parameter in the name of the parameter.
follow the guidelines described in Table 3-5 when naming types derived from or implementing certain .NET types.
add the suffix “Attribute” to names of custom attribute classes.
add the suffix “EventHandler” to names of delegates that are used in events.
add the suffix “Callback” to names of delegates other than those used as event handlers.
add the suffix “Delegate” to a delegate.
add the suffix “EventArgs.”
derive from this class; use the keyword supported by your language instead; for example, in C#, use the `enum` keyword.
add the suffix “Enum” or “Flag.”
add the suffix “Exception.”
add the suffix “Dictionary.” Note that `IDictionary` is a specific type of collection, but this guideline takes precedence over the more general collections guideline that follows.
add the suffix “Collection,” except for reusable, specialized data types such as “Queue” and “HashSet.”
add the suffix “Stream.”
use a singular type name for an enumeration unless its values are bit fields.
use a plural type name for an enumeration with bit fields as values, also called flags enum.
use an “Enum” suffix in enum type names.
use “Flag” or “Flags” suffixes in enum type names.
use a prefix on enumeration value names (e.g., “ad” for ADO enums, “rtf” for rich text enums).
give methods names that are verbs or verb phrases.
name properties using a noun, noun phrase, or adjective.
have properties that match the name of “Get” methods, such as a property named `TextWriter` and a method named `GetTextWriter`.
name collection properties with a plural phrase describing the items in the collection instead of using a singular phrase followed by “List” or “Collection.”
name Boolean properties with an affirmative phrase (`CanSeek` instead of `CantSeek`). Optionally, you can also prefix Boolean properties with “Is,” “Can,” or “Has,” but only where it adds value.
giving a property the same name as its type.
name events with a verb or a verb phrase.
give events names with a concept of before and after, using the present and past tenses, such as `Closing` and `Closed`.
use “Before” or “After” prefixes or postfixes to indicate pre- and post-events. Use present and past tenses as just described.
name event handlers (delegates used as types of events) with the “EventHandler” suffix, such as `ClickedEventHandler`.
use two parameters named *sender* and *e* in event handlers.
name event argument classes with the “EventArgs” suffix, as shown in the following example:
use PascalCasing in field names.
name fields using a noun, noun phrase, or adjective.
use a prefix for `public` or `protected` field names.
use camelCasing in parameter names.
use descriptive parameter names.
using names based on a parameter’s meaning rather than the parameter’s type.
use *left* and *right* for binary operator overload parameter names if there is no meaning to the parameters.
use *value* for unary operator overload parameter names if there is no meaning to the parameters.
meaningful names for operator overload parameters if doing so adds significant value.
use abbreviations or numeric indices for operator overload parameter names.
directly expose localizable resources as public (or protected) members.
ensure that each type is a well-defined set of related members, not just a random collection of unrelated functionality.
use namespaces to organize types into a hierarchy of related feature areas.
very deep namespace hierarchies. Such hierarchies are difficult to browse because the user has to backtrack often.
having too many namespaces.
having types designed for advanced scenarios in the same namespace as types intended for common programming tasks.
define types without specifying their namespaces.
defining a struct instead of a class if instances of the type are small and commonly short-lived or are commonly embedded in other objects, especially arrays.
defining a struct unless the type has all of the following characteristics:
favor defining classes over interfaces.
use abstract classes instead of interfaces to decouple the contract from implementations.
define an interface if you need to provide a polymorphic hierarchy of value types.
defining interfaces to achieve a similar effect to that of multiple inheritance.
define public or protected internal constructors in abstract types.
define a protected or an internal constructor in abstract classes.
provide at least one concrete type that inherits from each abstract class that you ship.
use static classes sparingly.
treat static classes as a miscellaneous bucket.
declare or override instance members in static classes.
declare static classes as sealed, abstract, and add a private instance constructor if your programming language does not have built-in support for static classes.
define an interface if you need some common API to be supported by a set of types that includes value types.
defining an interface if you need to support its functionality on types that already inherit from some other type.
using marker interfaces (interfaces with no members).
provide at least one type that is an implementation of an interface.
provide at least one API that consumes each interface you define (a method taking the interface as a parameter or a property typed as the interface).
add members to an interface that has previously shipped.
provide a default constructor for a struct.
define mutable value types.
declare immutable value types with the `readonly` modifier.
declare nonmutating methods on mutable value types with the `readonly` modifier.
ensure that a state where all instance data is set to zero, false, or null (as appropriate) is valid.
define ref-like value types (`ref struct` types), other than for specialized low-level purposes where performance is critical.
implement `IEquatable<T>` on value types.
explicitly extend `System.ValueType`. In fact, most languages prevent this.
use an enum to strongly type parameters, properties, and return values that represent sets of values.
favor using an enum instead of static constants.
use an enum for open sets (such as the operating system version, names of your friends, etc.).
provide reserved enum values that are intended for future use.
publicly exposing enums with only one value.
include sentinel values in enums.
provide a value of zero on simple enums.
using `Int32` (the default in most programming languages) as the underlying type of an enum unless any of the following is true:
name flag enums with plural nouns or noun phrases and simple enums with singular nouns or noun phrases.
extend `System.Enum` directly.
apply the `System.FlagsAttribute` to flag enums. Do not apply this attribute to simple enums.
use powers of 2 for the flag enum values so they can be freely combined using the bitwise OR operation.
providing special enum values for commonly used combinations of flags.
creating flag enums where certain combinations of values are invalid.
using flag enum values of zero unless the value represents “all flags are cleared” and is named appropriately, as prescribed by the next guideline.
name the zero value of flag enums `None`. For a flag enum, the value must always mean “all flags are cleared.”
adding values to enums, despite a small compatibility risk.
use nested types when the relationship between the nested type and its outer type is such that member-accessibility semantics are desirable.
use public nested types as a logical grouping construct; use namespaces for this purpose.

publicly exposed nested types. The only exception to this guideline is if variables of the nested type need to be declared only in rare scenarios such as subclassing or other advanced customization scenarios.
use nested types if the type is likely to be referenced outside of the containing type.
use nested types if they need to be instantiated by client code.
define a nested type as a member of an interface. Many languages do not support such a construct.
apply the `CLSCompliant(true)` attribute to assemblies with public types.
apply `AssemblyVersionAttribute` to assemblies with public types.
apply the following informational attributes to assemblies. These attributes are used by tools, such as Visual Studio, to inform the user of the assembly about its contents.

applying `ComVisible(false)` to your assembly. COM-callable APIs need to be designed explicitly. As a rule of thumb, .NET assemblies should not be visible to COM. If you do design the APIs to be COM-callable, you can apply `ComVisible(true)` either to the individual APIs or to the whole assembly.
applying `AssemblyFileVersionAttribute` and `Assembly-CopyrightAttribute` to provide additional information about the assembly.
using the format `<V>.<S>.<B>.<R>` for the assembly file version, where `V` is the major version number, `S` is the servicing number, `B` is the build number, and `R` is the build revision number.
defining a strongly typed string value type when a base class supports a fixed set of inputs but a derived type could support more.
declare a strongly typed string as an immutable value type (`struct`) with a string constructor.
override `ToString()` on a strongly typed string to return the underlying string value.
exposing the underlying string value from a strongly typed string in a get-only property.
override equality operators for strongly typed string types.
allow null inputs to the constructor of a strongly typed string.
declare known values for a strongly typed string via static get-only properties on the type.
creating overloads across `System.String` and a strongly typed string, unless the `System.String` overload was released in a previous version.
place the opening brace on the next line, indented to the same level as the block statement.
align the closing brace with the opening brace.
place the closing brace on its own line, except the end of a `do`..`while` statement.
omitting braces, even if the language allows it.
omitting braces in an argument validation preamble.
use the braceless variant of the `using` (dispose) statement.
using the braceless variant of the `await using` statement, except to simulate stacked `await using` statements with `ConfigureAwait`.
use one space before and after the opening and closing braces when they share a line with other code. Do not add a trailing space before a line break.
use a single space after a comma between parameters.
use a single space between arguments.
use spaces after the opening parenthesis or before the closing parenthesis.
use spaces between a member name and an opening parenthesis.
use spaces after or before square braces.
use spaces between flow control keywords and the open parenthesis.
use spaces before and after binary operators.
use spaces before or after unary operators.
use four consecutive space characters for indents.
use the tab character for indents.
indent contents of code blocks.
indent `case` blocks even if not using braces.
“outdent” `goto` labels one indentation level.
indent all continued lines of a single statement one indentation level.
chop before the first argument or parameter, indent one indentation level, and include one argument or parameter per line when a method declaration or method invocation is exceedingly long.
add a blank line before control flow statements.
add a blank line after a closing brace, unless the next line is also a closing brace.
add a blank line after “paragraphs” of code where it enhances readability.
always explicitly specify visibility modifiers.
specify the visibility modifier as the first modifier.
specify the `static` modifier immediately after visibility, for static members or static classes.
specify the `extern` method modifier immediately after the `static` modifier for an `extern` method.
specify the member slot modifier (`new`, `virtual`, `abstract`, `sealed`, or `override`) immediately after the `static` modifier (if specified).
specify the `readonly` modifier for fields or methods immediately after the member slot modifier (if specified).
specify the `unsafe` modifier for methods immediately after the `readonly` modifier (if specified).
specify the `volatile` modifier for fields immediately after the `static` modifier (if specified).
specify the `async` modifier as the last method modifier, when used.
use “`protected internal`” instead of “`internal protected`” for a member that can be called by derived types or types in the same assembly.
use “`private protected`” instead of “`protected private`” for a member that can be called by derived types within the same assembly.
add the optional trailing comma after the last enum member.
add the optional trailing comma after a property assignment from an object initializer, or addition via a collection initializer, when the initializer spans multiple lines.
use `this.` unless absolutely necessary.
use language keywords (`string`, `int`, `double`, …) instead of BCL type names (`String`, `Int32`, `Double`, …), for both variable declarations and method invocation.
use the `var` keyword except to save the result of a `new`, `as`-cast or “hard” cast.
use object initializers where possible.
use collection initializers where possible.
using expression-bodied members when the implementation of a property or method is unlikely to change.
use auto-implemented properties when the implementation is unlikely to change.
restrict code to ASCII characters, and use Unicode escape sequences (`\uXXXX`) when needed for non-ASCII values.
use the `nameof(...)` syntax, instead of a literal string, when referring to the name of a type, member, or parameter.
apply the `readonly` modifier to fields when possible.
use `if`…`throw` instead of assignment–expression–throw for argument validation.
follow the Framework Design Guidelines for naming identifiers, except for naming private and internal fields.
use PascalCasing for namespace, type, and member names, except for internal and private fields.
use PascalCasing for const locals and const fields except for interop code, where it should match the name from the called code exactly.
use camelCasing for private and internal fields.
use a prefix “_” (underscore) for private and internal instance fields, “s_” for private and internal static fields, and “t_” for private and internal thread-static fields.
use camelCasing for local variables.
use camelCasing for parameters.
use Hungarian notation (i.e., do not encode the type of a variable in its name).
use comments unless they describe something not obvious to someone other than the developer who wrote the code.
multiline syntax (`/* ... */`) for comments. The single-line syntax (`// ...`) is preferred even when a comment spans multiple lines.
place comments at the end of a line unless the comment is very short.
placing comments at the end of a line even when the comment is very short.
writing “I” in comments.
have more than one public type in a source file, unless they differ only in the number of generic parameters or one is nested in the other.
name the source file with the name of the public type it contains.
name the source file for a `partial` type with the name of the primary file and a logical description of the contents of the file separated by a “.” (period), such as “JsonDocument.Parse.cs”.
organize the directory hierarchy just like the namespace hierarchy.
